tagline.text: A bay of jungle and sea at an old naval base, where families play together

location.label: Location
location.text: Subic Bay Freeport Zone, Olongapo, Zambales Province

children.text: A deep bay that served as a Spanish and then American naval base for about a century has become a freeport zone, great for families to enjoy primeval jungle experiences, a marine theme park, a safari, World War II wreck diving, and quiet beaches.

Subic Bay is a natural bay cutting deep into Luzon's west coast, between the Zambales mountain range and the Bataan Peninsula. Deep waters and calm seas, sheltered by surrounding mountains, led the 19th-century Spanish navy to build a shipyard here, and from

the United States took it over and grew it into one of the largest overseas naval bases in the Pacific. During the Korean and Vietnam wars, it was a key supply and repair base for the U.S. Pacific Fleet. When the Philippine Senate refused to extend the base agreement in
, U.S. forces left in
November 1992
, and the base was converted into the Subic Bay Freeport Zone (SBMA).

The base era's straight roads, wide lawns, and old naval buildings lining the coast are now used as hotels, restaurants, a yacht club, and duty-free shops. Traffic law enforcement is strict and the streets are clean inside the freeport zone, giving it a noticeably different atmosphere from other Philippine cities. Right next door is Olongapo City, which thrived during the base era and offers a contrasting scene with its down-to-earth markets and eateries.

Subic's real charm is the nature spread out right behind the city. Having escaped development as a military reserve during the base era, the Subic tropical rainforest is one of Luzon's finest surviving lowland forests, home to Philippine endemic birds and colonies of the golden-crowned flying fox, among the world's largest bats. The indigenous Aeta people have a history of teaching jungle survival skills to the U.S. Marines, and today they pass that knowledge on to tourists.

Beneath the water lie shipwrecks sunk during the Spanish-American War and World War II, making this one of the best wreck-diving destinations in Southeast Asia. With jungle experiences, a marine theme park, a safari, beaches, and duty-free shopping all in one place, it's especially well suited to family trips with children and weekend getaways during a stay in Manila or Clark.
A marine theme park connected directly to the sea, popular for its dolphin and sea lion shows and hands-on programs. The swim-with-dolphins program requires a separate booking.
A zoo featuring a tiger safari ride that takes you through an enclosure for a close-up view of tigers, plus a crocodile farm and an animal encounter area. Half a day is enough to see it all.

An Aeta instructor demonstrates jungle survival skills such as cooking rice in bamboo, making fire, and finding edible plants. You can walk through the actual forest on trails run by the Aeta community, such as the Pamulaklakin forest trail.
A zipline and canopy course over the tropical forest, with separate routes for children and adults to enjoy.
The USS New York, an armored cruiser scuttled in
to keep it from falling into Japanese hands, is a massive
-long wreck lying at a depth of about
. There are many wrecks accessible to beginners as well, such as El Capitan at a depth of about
and the San Quintin, scuttled by Spain in
to block the bay entrance.
Enjoy sunset at SBMA Beach along the freeport zone's coastal road, take a boat out to Grande Island at the mouth of the bay, or go swimming at the quiet Camayan Beach, reachable by car.
There's a spot where you can watch the spectacle of thousands of fruit bats taking flight from the forest at dusk. Observe quietly to help protect their habitat.

On the third day, continue on with camping at Anawangin Cove or a Mount Pinatubo tour, or head over to Clark to enjoy a Kapampangan food trip.
From Manila, take NLEX up and switch to SCTEX, then exit at Tipo to enter the freeport zone. It's about

2.5–3 hours
, with toll costs of about
one way. From Clark, it's about
1 hour
via SCTEX. Inside the freeport zone, speed limits, seatbelt use, and a ban on phone use while driving are strictly enforced.
Take a bus bound for Olongapo from a Victory Liner terminal in Cubao, Pasay, or Caloocan. It's about
3–4 hours
, with fares around
. From the Olongapo terminal, get to a hotel inside the freeport zone by taxi or tricycle (as far as the zone boundary). Coming from Clark, take an Olongapo-bound bus from the Dau terminal, about
1.5–2 hours
If flying directly from Korea, Clark International Airport (CRK) is the closest, and it's about
1 hour
by car from the airport to Subic. Subic Bay International Airport currently has almost no regular passenger routes.
Attractions inside the freeport zone are spread far apart, so a rental car or daily vehicle charter (about
) is most convenient. There are also authorized taxis that operate within the zone; confirm the fare in advance. Around the beaches and waterfront, renting a bicycle is a nice way to get around.
The Zambales coast, home to Subic, is one of the Philippines' regions with the most clear-cut dry and wet seasons. In the
November–May
dry season, there's almost no rain and the sea is calm, making it great for beaches, island outings, and diving alike.
December–February
in particular is cool and clear, pleasant for touring outdoor theme parks.
March–May
is hot, but the water is warm and visibility is good, making it peak diving season.
During the
June–October
wet season, the southwest monsoon (Habagat) blows straight into the west coast, and most of the year's rainfall is concentrated in this period.
July–September
can see days of heavy rain in a row, and when a typhoon comes, boat trips and diving stop entirely. Theme parks and shopping are still possible, but it's best to leave beach plans open.
During long holidays, Holy Week, and summer vacation (
April–May
), hotels fill up with families visiting from Manila and Clark. Going on a weekday means much shorter waits at the theme parks.

Accommodation clusters along the Waterfront Road inside the freeport zone. There are hotels converted from old naval officer quarters, resorts overlooking the bay, and family-friendly condotels, running about
a night. Forest resorts or boutique hotels near the yacht harbor are good for a quiet stay. To save on budget, you can use budget-to-midrange lodging (about
a night) in Olongapo town or nearby Barrio Barretto Beach.

Reflecting the base era, Subic has many American-style steak, burger, and barbecue restaurants, and restaurants overlooking the sea line up around the yacht harbor for seafood. In Olongapo town, you can enjoy cheap Filipino seafood and down-to-earth eateries. At the duty-free shops, you can buy imported American and Australian food and wine relatively cheaply, drawing expats who come to stock up. Since the area once hosted a large Korean shipyard, there are also a few Korean restaurants and Korean grocery stores.
Zoobic Safari and Ocean Adventure often have online advance purchases or bundle discounts cheaper than the on-site price.
Enter the theme parks early in the morning. In the afternoon, tour groups crowd in and the midday heat makes the animals sluggish too.
Driving rules are strict inside the freeport zone. Speeding, not wearing a seatbelt, and using a phone while driving are all immediately enforced.
For the jungle trails, bring long pants, sneakers, and insect repellent. Long socks are good during the wet season, when leeches appear.
If you're planning to dive, use a local shop experienced with wrecks. For the deep USS New York, Advanced certification or higher is recommended.
There are purchase limits and passport-check rules at the duty-free shops, so bring your passport.
The waterfront coastal road at sunset is the highlight of a trip to Subic. Take a walk or bike ride around
5 PM
The checkpoint between Olongapo town and the freeport zone gets congested at rush hour, so allow extra travel time.
During heavy wet-season rain, jungle trails and valleys carry a risk of flash floods and landslides. If management restricts access, don't push your way in.
Always follow the staff's instructions for animal encounters at Zoobic Safari. Don't put your hands or food out the window.
Subic Bay has strong currents and heavy vessel traffic. Avoid swimming outside designated beach areas.
Fruit bats are a protected species. Don't disturb their habitat with noise or light, and avoid drone photography as well.
In Olongapo town, watch out for pickpockets and inflated prices, and don't walk around alone late at night.
During typhoon season, low-lying coastal areas can flood. Check weather warnings regularly.
